title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Money, Considered as a Particular Branch of the Society's General Stock, or the Expense of Maintaining the National Capital

The First Book showed that the price of most commodities breaks down into three parts. One part pays the wages of labour, another the profits on the capital invested, and a third the rent of the land used to produce the goods and bring them to market. A few commodities have a price made up of only two of these parts, the wages of labour and the profits of capital, and a very few have a price that consists entirely of one, the wages of labour. But the price of every commodity necessarily resolves into one, two, or all three of these parts. Any portion of it that goes neither to rent nor to wages must be profit to somebody.

Since this is true of every individual commodity taken on its own, it must also be true of all the commodities that together make up a country's whole annual produce of land and labour, taken collectively. The total price, or exchangeable value, of that annual produce must break down into the same three parts and be shared out among the country's inhabitants, either as wages for their labour, profits on their capital, or rent on their land.

Yet although the whole value of a country's annual produce is divided among its inhabitants in this way and provides them with an income, we can make a distinction here just as we do with the rent of a private estate, where we separate the gross rent from the net rent. The same distinction applies to the combined income of all the inhabitants of a great country.

The gross rent of a private estate is everything the tenant farmer pays. The net rent is what is left for the landlord after deducting the cost of management, repairs, and all other necessary charges. In other words, the net rent is what he can afford to set aside in his stock for immediate consumption, or spend on his table, his carriage and horses, the ornaments of his house and furniture, and his private pleasures and amusements, without damaging the estate itself. His real wealth is measured not by his gross rent but by his net rent.

The gross revenue of all the inhabitants of a great country is the whole annual produce of their land and labour. The net revenue is what is left over for them after deducting the cost of maintaining first their fixed capital and second their circulating capital. In other words, it is what they can set aside in their stock for immediate consumption, or spend on their subsistence, comforts, and amusements, without eating into their capital. Their real wealth too is measured not by their gross revenue but by their net revenue.

The whole cost of maintaining the fixed capital must clearly be excluded from the net revenue of the society. The materials needed to keep up their useful machines and tools of trade, their profitable buildings, and so on, can never form any part of it, and neither can the produce of the labour needed to shape those materials into the proper form. The price of that labour may indeed form part of the net revenue, because the workmen employed in this way can put the whole value of their wages into their stock for immediate consumption. But with other kinds of labour, both the price and the produce go into this stock: the price into the stock of the workmen, the produce into the stock of other people, whose subsistence, comforts, and amusements are increased by those workmen's labour.

The purpose of fixed capital is to increase the productive power of labour, or to let the same number of workers do far more work. On a farm where all the necessary buildings, fences, drains, roads, and so on are in perfect order, the same number of labourers and working cattle will raise a far greater produce than on a farm of equal size with equally good soil but without these conveniences. In manufacturing, the same number of hands working with the best machinery will turn out far more goods than they would with cruder tools of trade. Money properly spent on fixed capital of any kind is always repaid with great profit, and it increases the annual produce by far more than the cost of keeping up these improvements. That upkeep, however, still requires a certain share of the produce. A certain quantity of materials, and the labour of a certain number of workmen, both of which could have been used directly to add to the food, clothing, and lodging, the subsistence and comforts of the society, are instead diverted to another use, a highly advantageous one but still a different one. This is why every improvement in mechanics that lets the same number of workmen do the same amount of work with cheaper and simpler machinery than before is always regarded as a benefit to society. A certain quantity of materials, and the labour of a certain number of workmen, that had been used to support a more complex and expensive machine can afterwards be applied to increasing the work that this or any other machinery exists only to perform. Suppose the owner of some great manufactory spends a thousand pounds a year maintaining his machinery. If he can cut that cost to five hundred, he will naturally spend the other five hundred on buying more materials to be worked up by additional workmen. So the work that his machinery exists only to perform will naturally increase, and with it all the advantage and convenience that society can draw from that work.

The cost of maintaining the fixed capital of a great country can fairly be compared to the cost of repairs on a private estate. Repairs are often necessary to keep up the produce of the estate, and therefore to keep up both the gross and the net rent of the landlord. But when better management lets that cost be reduced without any drop in produce, the gross rent stays at least the same as before, while the net rent necessarily rises.

Although the whole cost of maintaining the fixed capital must therefore be excluded from the net revenue of the society, the same is not true of the cost of maintaining the circulating capital. This second kind of capital is made up of four parts: money, provisions, materials, and finished goods. The last three, as already noted, are regularly drawn out of the circulating capital and placed either in the society's fixed capital or in its stock for immediate consumption. Whatever portion of those consumable goods is not used to maintain the fixed capital goes entirely into the stock for consumption and forms part of the society's net revenue. So maintaining these three parts of the circulating capital takes no portion of the annual produce away from the net revenue beyond what is needed to maintain the fixed capital.

In this respect a society's circulating capital differs from an individual's. An individual's circulating capital is entirely excluded from forming any part of his net revenue, which must consist wholly of his profits. But although every individual's circulating capital forms part of the society's, it is not on that account entirely excluded from also forming part of the society's net revenue. The whole stock of goods in a merchant's shop must by no means be placed in his own stock for immediate consumption, yet it may be placed in the stock of other people, who, drawing an income from other sources, can regularly repay him their value together with his profit, without reducing either his capital or theirs.
Money, therefore, is the only part of a society's circulating capital whose maintenance can cause any reduction in its net revenue.
The fixed capital, and the part of the circulating capital that consists of money, bear a very strong resemblance to one another in the way they affect the society's revenue.

First, those machines and tools of trade require a certain expense, first to build them and then to keep them up, and both of these expenses, though they form part of the gross revenue, are deductions from the net revenue of the society. In the same way, the stock of money that circulates in any country requires a certain expense, first to gather it and then to maintain it, and both of these expenses too, though they form part of the gross revenue, are deductions from the net revenue. A certain quantity of very valuable materials, gold and silver, and of very skilled labour, instead of adding to the stock for immediate consumption, the subsistence, comforts, and amusements of individuals, is used to support that great but expensive instrument of commerce. It is through that instrument that every individual in the society has his subsistence, comforts, and amusements regularly delivered to him in their proper proportions.

Second, just as the machines and tools of trade that make up the fixed capital, whether of an individual or of a society, form no part of either the gross or the net revenue, so money, which regularly distributes the whole revenue of the society among all its members, itself forms no part of that revenue. The great wheel of circulation is entirely different from the goods that are circulated by means of it. The revenue of the society consists wholly in those goods, not in the wheel that circulates them. In working out either the gross or the net revenue of any society, we must always deduct, from the whole annual circulation of money and goods, the entire value of the money, of which not a single farthing can ever form part of either.
Only the ambiguity of language can make this statement seem doubtful or paradoxical. Once it is properly explained and understood, it is almost self-evident.

When we talk about a particular sum of money, we sometimes mean nothing more than the metal coins it is made of, and sometimes we include in our meaning a vague reference to the goods it can buy, or to the purchasing power that owning it conveys. So when we say that the circulating money of England has been estimated at eighteen million, we mean only the amount of metal coins that some writers have calculated, or rather guessed, to circulate in the country. But when we say that a man is worth fifty or a hundred pounds a year, we usually mean to express not only the amount of metal coins paid to him each year but the value of the goods he can buy or consume in a year. We usually mean to indicate what his way of living is, or ought to be, the quantity and quality of the necessities and comforts of life he can properly allow himself.

When by a particular sum of money we mean not only the amount of metal coins it is made of but also a vague reference to the goods it can buy, the wealth or revenue it then stands for is equal to only one of the two values that the same word ambiguously suggests, and more properly to the second than to the first, to the money's worth rather than to the money.

So if a guinea is a particular person's weekly pension, he can buy with it, over the course of the week, a certain quantity of subsistence, comforts, and amusements. The greater or smaller that quantity is, the greater or smaller are his real riches, his real weekly income. His weekly income is certainly not equal to both the guinea and what can be bought with it, but only to one or the other of those two equal values, and more properly to the second than to the first, to the guinea's worth rather than to the guinea itself.

If such a person's pension were paid to him not in gold but in a weekly note for a guinea, his income would surely consist not so much in the piece of paper as in what he could get for it. A guinea can be thought of as a note for a certain quantity of necessities and comforts, drawn on all the tradesmen in the neighbourhood. The income of the person it is paid to consists not so much in the piece of gold as in what he can get for it, or what he can exchange it for. If it could be exchanged for nothing, it would, like a note drawn on a bankrupt, be worth no more than the most useless scrap of paper.

In the same way, although the weekly or yearly income of all the different inhabitants of a country may be, and often actually is, paid to them in money, their real riches, the real weekly or yearly income of all of them taken together, must always be great or small in proportion to the quantity of consumable goods they can all buy with that money. The whole income of all of them together is clearly not equal to both the money and the consumable goods, but only to one or the other of those two values, and more properly to the second than to the first.

So although we often express a person's income by the metal coins paid to him each year, this is only because the amount of those coins sets the limit of his purchasing power, the value of the goods he can afford to consume in a year. We still regard his income as consisting in that power to purchase or consume, not in the coins that convey it.

If this is clear enough even for an individual, it is clearer still for a society. The amount of metal coins paid to an individual each year is often exactly equal to his income, and so it is the shortest and best expression of its value. But the amount of metal coins circulating in a society can never equal the income of all its members. Since the same guinea that pays one man's weekly pension today may pay another's tomorrow and a third man's the day after, the amount of metal coins circulating in any country each year must always be worth far less than the whole of the money pensions paid with them. But the purchasing power, the goods that can be bought one after another with the whole of those money pensions as they are paid out, must always be worth exactly the same as those pensions, and so must the income of the different people they are paid to. That income, therefore, cannot consist in those metal coins, whose total amount is so much less than its value, but in the purchasing power, in the goods that can be bought one after another with the coins as they pass from hand to hand.

Money, therefore, the great wheel of circulation, the great instrument of commerce, like all other tools of trade, forms part, and a very valuable part, of the capital, but it forms no part of the revenue of the society it belongs to. Although the metal coins it is made of distribute to every man, in the course of their yearly circulation, the income that properly belongs to him, the coins themselves form no part of that income.

Third and last, the machines and tools of trade that make up the fixed capital resemble the money part of the circulating capital in one further way. Just as every saving in the cost of building and maintaining those machines that does not reduce the productive power of labour is an improvement to the net revenue of the society, so every saving in the cost of gathering and maintaining the money part of the circulating capital is an improvement of exactly the same kind.

It is clear enough, and has partly been explained already, how every saving in the cost of supporting the fixed capital improves the net revenue of the society. The whole capital of any business owner is necessarily divided between his fixed capital and his circulating capital. As long as his total capital stays the same, the smaller one part is, the larger the other must be. It is the circulating capital that supplies the materials and the wages of labour and sets industry in motion. So every saving in the cost of maintaining the fixed capital that does not reduce the productive power of labour must increase the fund that sets industry in motion, and therefore the annual produce of land and labour, the real revenue of every society.

Putting paper in place of gold and silver money replaces a very expensive instrument of commerce with one that is much cheaper, and sometimes equally convenient. Circulation comes to be carried on by a new wheel that costs less both to build and to maintain than the old one. But exactly how this works, and how it tends to increase either the gross or the net revenue of the society, is not so obvious, and may therefore need some further explanation.
There are several different kinds of paper money, but the circulating notes of banks and bankers are the kind best known and best suited to this purpose.

When the people of a particular country have such confidence in a particular banker's wealth, honesty, and good judgement that they believe he is always ready to pay on demand whatever promissory notes are likely to be presented to him at any time, those notes come to circulate just like gold and silver money, because people are confident that such money can be had for them at any time.

Suppose a particular banker lends his customers his own promissory notes up to a total of a hundred thousand pounds. Since those notes serve all the purposes of money, his borrowers pay him the same interest as if he had lent them that much money. This interest is the source of his profit. Although some of those notes are always coming back to him for payment, some of them keep circulating for months and years at a time. So even though he generally has notes worth a hundred thousand pounds in circulation, twenty thousand pounds in gold and silver may often be enough to meet the occasional demands. By this operation, then, twenty thousand pounds in gold and silver perform all the functions that a hundred thousand could otherwise have performed. The same exchanges can be made, and the same quantity of consumable goods can be circulated and delivered to their proper consumers, by means of his promissory notes worth a hundred thousand pounds, as could be done with an equal value of gold and silver money. In this way eighty thousand pounds of gold and silver can be spared from the country's circulation. And if many different banks and bankers carry on operations of the same kind at the same time, the whole circulation can be conducted with only a fifth of the gold and silver that would otherwise have been needed.

Suppose, for example, that the whole circulating money of some particular country amounted at a given time to one million sterling, that sum being then enough to circulate the whole annual produce of its land and labour. Suppose too that some time later, various banks and bankers issued promissory notes payable to the bearer up to a total of one million, keeping two hundred thousand pounds in their various vaults to meet occasional demands. There would then remain in circulation eight hundred thousand pounds in gold and silver, plus a million in banknotes, or eighteen hundred thousand pounds of paper and metal money together. But the country's annual produce of land and labour had previously needed only one million to circulate and deliver it to its proper consumers, and that annual produce cannot be increased right away by these banking operations. So one million will still be enough to circulate it afterwards. Since the goods being bought and sold are exactly the same as before, the same quantity of money will be enough to buy and sell them. The channel of circulation, if I may use that expression, will stay exactly the same as before. We have supposed one million to be enough to fill that channel. So whatever is poured into it beyond that sum cannot run through it but must overflow. One million eight hundred thousand pounds are poured in, so eight hundred thousand pounds must overflow, that being more than the country's circulation can use. But although this sum cannot be used at home, it is too valuable to lie idle. It will therefore be sent abroad to seek the profitable employment it cannot find at home. The paper, however, cannot go abroad, because far from the banks that issue it, and outside the country where payment can be legally demanded, it will not be accepted in ordinary payments. So gold and silver worth eight hundred thousand pounds will be sent abroad, and the channel of home circulation will remain filled with a million in paper instead of the million in metal that filled it before.

But although such a great quantity of gold and silver is sent abroad in this way, we must not imagine it is sent for nothing, or that its owners make a present of it to foreign nations. They will exchange it for foreign goods of one kind or another, in order to supply the consumption either of some other foreign country or of their own.

If they use it to buy goods in one foreign country in order to supply the consumption of another, in what is called the carrying trade, whatever profit they make will be added to the net revenue of their own country. It is like a new fund created to carry on a new trade, with domestic business now transacted by paper and the gold and silver turned into a fund for this new trade.

If they use it to buy foreign goods for home consumption, they can do one of two things. First, they can buy goods likely to be consumed by idle people who produce nothing, such as foreign wines, foreign silks, and the like. Or second, they can buy an additional stock of materials, tools, and provisions in order to maintain and employ more industrious people, who reproduce the value of their annual consumption with a profit.

To the extent that it is used in the first way, it encourages extravagance, increases spending and consumption without increasing production or setting up any lasting fund to support that spending, and is in every way harmful to the society.

To the extent that it is used in the second way, it encourages industry. Although it increases the society's consumption, it provides a lasting fund to support that consumption, since the people who consume reproduce with a profit the whole value of their annual consumption. The gross revenue of the society, the annual produce of its land and labour, is increased by the whole value that those workmen's labour adds to the materials they work on, and its net revenue is increased by whatever is left of that value after deducting what is needed to keep up the tools and instruments of their trade.

That the greater part of the gold and silver forced abroad by these banking operations, and used to buy foreign goods for home consumption, is and must be used to buy goods of this second kind seems not only likely but almost unavoidable. Although some particular men may sometimes increase their spending a great deal even though their income does not rise at all, we can be sure that no whole class or order of men ever does so. For although common prudence does not always govern the conduct of every individual, it always influences the conduct of the majority within every class or order. But the income of idle people, considered as a class or order, cannot be increased in the slightest by these banking operations. So their spending in general cannot be much increased by them, though that of a few individuals among them may be, and sometimes actually is. Since the demand of idle people for foreign goods stays the same, or very nearly the same as before, only a very small part of the money forced abroad by these banking operations and used to buy foreign goods for home consumption is likely to be spent on goods for their use. The greater part of it will naturally be destined to employ industry, not to support idleness.

When we work out how much industry the circulating capital of any society can employ, we must always look only at the parts of it that consist of provisions, materials, and finished goods. The other part, which consists of money and serves only to circulate those three, must always be deducted. To set industry in motion, three things are needed: materials to work on, tools to work with, and the wages, the reward for which the work is done. Money is neither a material to work on nor a tool to work with. And although the workman's wages are usually paid to him in money, his real income, like that of all other men, consists not in the money but in the money's worth, not in the metal coins but in what can be got for them.

The quantity of industry that any capital can employ must clearly equal the number of workmen it can supply with materials, tools, and a maintenance suited to the nature of the work. Money may be needed to buy the materials and tools of the work, as well as the maintenance of the workmen. But the quantity of industry that the whole capital can employ is certainly not equal to both the money that buys and the materials, tools, and maintenance bought with it, but only to one or the other of those two values, and more properly to the second than to the first.

When paper is put in place of gold and silver money, the quantity of materials, tools, and maintenance that the whole circulating capital can supply may be increased by the whole value of the gold and silver that used to be spent on buying them. The whole value of the great wheel of circulation and distribution is added to the goods that are circulated and distributed by means of it. The operation somewhat resembles that of the owner of some great work who, thanks to an improvement in mechanics, dismantles his old machinery and adds the difference between its price and that of the new machinery to his circulating capital, to the fund from which he supplies materials and wages to his workmen.

What proportion the circulating money of any country bears to the whole value of the annual produce circulated by means of it is perhaps impossible to determine. Different authors have estimated it at a fifth, a tenth, a twentieth, and a thirtieth of that value. But however small the proportion the circulating money bears to the whole value of the annual produce, since only a part, and often only a small part, of that produce is ever destined to maintain industry, the money must always bear a very considerable proportion to that part. So when the substitution of paper reduces the gold and silver needed for circulation to perhaps a fifth of the former quantity, if even the greater part of the other four-fifths is added to the funds destined to maintain industry, it must make a very considerable addition to the quantity of that industry, and therefore to the value of the annual produce of land and labour.

An operation of this kind has, within the past twenty-five or thirty years, been carried out in Scotland by the founding of new banking companies in almost every sizeable town, and even in some country villages. Its effects have been exactly those described above. The business of the country is now carried on almost entirely by means of the paper of these various banking companies, with which purchases and payments of all kinds are commonly made. Silver hardly ever appears, except as change for a twenty-shilling banknote, and gold still less often. But although the conduct of all these different companies has not been beyond reproach, and has accordingly required an act of parliament to regulate it, the country has clearly drawn great benefit from their trade. I have heard it claimed that the trade of the city of Glasgow doubled within about fifteen years after the first banks were set up there, and that the trade of Scotland has more than quadrupled since the first two public banks were established at Edinburgh, one of which, called the Bank of Scotland, was set up by act of parliament in 1695, and the other, called the Royal Bank, by royal charter in 1727. Whether the trade of Scotland in general, or of the city of Glasgow in particular, has really grown by so great a proportion in so short a period, I do not claim to know. If either has grown by this proportion, it seems an effect too great to be explained by the operation of this single cause. But that the trade and industry of Scotland have grown very considerably over this period, and that the banks have contributed a good deal to that growth, cannot be doubted.

The value of the silver money that circulated in Scotland before the Union of 1707, and that was brought into the Bank of Scotland immediately afterwards to be recoined, came to £411,117 10s. 9d. sterling. No account has been found of the gold coin, but it appears from the old records of the Scottish mint that the value of the gold coined each year somewhat exceeded that of the silver. There were also a good many people on this occasion who, mistrusting repayment, did not bring their silver into the Bank of Scotland, and there was besides some English coin that was not called in. So the whole value of the gold and silver circulating in Scotland before the Union cannot be reckoned at less than a million sterling. It seems to have made up almost the entire circulation of the country, for although the circulation of the Bank of Scotland, which then had no rival, was considerable, it seems to have formed only a very small part of the whole. Today the whole circulation of Scotland cannot be reckoned at less than two million, of which the part consisting of gold and silver most probably does not come to half a million. But although the circulating gold and silver of Scotland have shrunk so greatly over this period, its real riches and prosperity do not appear to have suffered at all. On the contrary, its agriculture, manufactures, and trade, the annual produce of its land and labour, have clearly grown.

It is chiefly by discounting bills of exchange, that is, by advancing money on them before they fall due, that most banks and bankers issue their promissory notes. On whatever sum they advance, they always deduct the legal interest up to the date the bill falls due. When the bill is paid at maturity, it repays the bank the value of what was advanced, together with a clear profit equal to the interest. A banker who advances to the merchant whose bill he discounts not gold and silver but his own promissory notes has the advantage of being able to discount a greater amount, by the whole value of his promissory notes that he finds, by experience, are usually in circulation. He is thereby able to earn his clear gain of interest on so much larger a sum.

The commerce of Scotland, which even now is not very great, was even smaller when the first two banking companies were set up, and those companies would have had little business had they confined themselves to discounting bills of exchange. So they invented another way of issuing their promissory notes, by granting what they call cash accounts. This meant giving credit up to a certain sum, two or three thousand pounds for example, to any individual who could find two persons of undoubted credit and good landed estate to stand surety for him, guaranteeing that whatever money was advanced to him, within the agreed credit limit, would be repaid on demand together with the legal interest. Credits of this kind are, I believe, commonly granted by banks and bankers all over the world. But the easy terms on which the Scottish banking companies accept repayment are, so far as I know, peculiar to them, and have perhaps been the main cause both of the great trade of these companies and of the benefit the country has gained from it.

Anyone who has a credit of this kind with one of these companies, and borrows, say, a thousand pounds on it, can repay the sum bit by bit, twenty or thirty pounds at a time, with the company deducting a proportionate part of the interest on the large sum from the day each of these small sums is paid in, until the whole is repaid in this way. So all merchants, and almost all men of business, find it convenient to keep such cash accounts with the banks, and are thereby interested in promoting the trade of these companies by readily accepting their notes in all payments, and by encouraging everyone they have any influence over to do the same. When their customers come to them for money, the banks generally advance it in their own promissory notes. The merchants pay these away to the manufacturers for goods, the manufacturers to the farmers for materials and provisions, the farmers to their landlords for rent. The landlords repay them to the merchants for the comforts and luxuries the merchants supply, and the merchants return them again to the banks to balance their cash accounts or to repay what they have borrowed. In this way almost the whole money business of the country is transacted by means of these notes. Hence the great trade of these companies.

By means of these cash accounts, every merchant can, without imprudence, carry on a larger trade than he otherwise could. Suppose there are two merchants, one in London and the other in Edinburgh, who employ equal capitals in the same branch of trade. The Edinburgh merchant can, without imprudence, carry on a larger trade and give work to more people than the London merchant. The London merchant must always keep by him a considerable sum of money, either in his own coffers or in those of his banker, who pays him no interest on it, in order to meet the demands continually coming in for payment of the goods he buys on credit. Let the usual amount of this sum be five hundred pounds. The value of the goods in his warehouse must then always be five hundred pounds less than it would have been if he had not been obliged to keep such a sum idle. Suppose he generally sells his whole stock on hand, or goods to the value of his whole stock, once a year. By being forced to keep so large a sum idle, he must sell five hundred pounds' worth less goods in a year than he otherwise could. His annual profits must be less by all he could have made from selling five hundred pounds' worth more goods, and the number of people employed in preparing his goods for market must be less by all those that five hundred pounds more capital could have employed. The Edinburgh merchant, on the other hand, keeps no money idle to meet such occasional demands. When they actually arise, he meets them from his cash account with the bank, and gradually repays the sum borrowed with the money or paper that comes in from the occasional sales of his goods. So with the same capital he can, without imprudence, keep a larger quantity of goods in his warehouse at all times than the London merchant, and can thereby both make a greater profit himself and give steady work to a greater number of industrious people who prepare those goods for market. Hence the great benefit the country has drawn from this trade.

It may be thought that the ease of discounting bills of exchange gives English merchants a convenience equivalent to the cash accounts of the Scottish merchants. But it must be remembered that the Scottish merchants can discount their bills of exchange just as easily as the English merchants, and on top of that have the added convenience of their cash accounts.

The whole paper money of every kind that can easily circulate in any country can never exceed the value of the gold and silver it takes the place of, or that (assuming the same amount of commerce) would circulate there if there were no paper money. If twenty-shilling notes, for example, are the lowest paper money current in Scotland, the whole of that currency that can easily circulate there cannot exceed the sum of gold and silver that would be needed to carry out the annual exchanges of twenty shillings' value and upwards usually transacted within the country. Should the circulating paper at any time exceed that sum, then since the excess could neither be sent abroad nor used in the country's circulation, it must immediately return to the banks to be exchanged for gold and silver. Many people would at once notice that they had more of this paper than they needed for their business at home, and since they could not send it abroad, they would immediately demand payment for it from the banks. Once this surplus paper was turned into gold and silver, they could easily find a use for it by sending it abroad, but they could find none while it stayed in the form of paper. There would therefore be an immediate run on the banks to the full extent of this surplus paper, and if the banks showed any difficulty or reluctance in paying, to a much greater extent, since the alarm this caused would necessarily increase the run.

Over and above the expenses common to every branch of trade, such as house rent and the wages of servants, clerks, accountants, and so on, the expenses peculiar to a bank consist chiefly of two items. The first is the cost of keeping at all times in its coffers, to meet the occasional demands of its noteholders, a large sum of money on which it loses the interest. The second is the cost of refilling those coffers as fast as they are emptied by meeting such demands.

A banking company that issues more paper than the country's circulation can use, and whose excess is continually returning for payment, ought to increase the quantity of gold and silver it keeps at all times in its coffers, not just in proportion to this excessive increase in its circulation but in a much greater proportion, since its notes return upon it much faster than in proportion to the excess of their quantity. Such a company, therefore, ought to increase the first item of its expense not just in proportion to this forced increase of its business but in a much greater proportion.

The coffers of such a company, too, though they ought to be kept much fuller, will yet empty themselves much faster than if its business were kept within more reasonable bounds, and will require not only a more violent but a more constant and unbroken outlay to refill them. The coin that is thus continually drawn in such large quantities from its coffers cannot be used in the country's circulation. It takes the place of paper that is already more than the circulation can use, and so it too is more than the circulation can use. But since that coin will not be allowed to lie idle, it must in one form or another be sent abroad to find the profitable employment it cannot find at home. And this continual export of gold and silver, by making it harder, must necessarily increase still further the bank's expense of finding new gold and silver to refill coffers that empty themselves so rapidly. Such a company, therefore, must, in proportion to this forced increase of its business, increase the second item of its expense even more than the first.

Suppose that all the paper of a particular bank that the country's circulation can easily absorb and use comes to exactly forty thousand pounds, and that to meet occasional demands this bank is obliged to keep ten thousand pounds in gold and silver in its coffers at all times. Should this bank try to circulate forty-four thousand pounds, the four thousand pounds over and above what the circulation can easily absorb and use will return upon it almost as fast as they are issued. To meet occasional demands, therefore, this bank ought to keep in its coffers at all times not eleven thousand pounds only but fourteen thousand pounds. It will thus gain nothing from the interest on the four thousand pounds of excessive circulation, and it will lose the whole expense of continually collecting four thousand pounds in gold and silver, which will be continually going out of its coffers as fast as they are brought in.

Had every individual banking company always understood and attended to its own particular interest, the circulation could never have been overstocked with paper money. But not every banking company has always understood or attended to its own particular interest, and the circulation has frequently been overstocked with paper money.

Because it issued too much paper, and because the surplus kept coming back to be exchanged for gold and silver, the Bank of England was obliged for many years running to coin gold worth between eight hundred thousand pounds and a million a year, or about eight hundred and fifty thousand pounds on average. The gold coin had fallen into such a worn and degraded state a few years earlier that, to mint all this new money, the bank often had to buy gold bullion at the high price of four pounds an ounce and then issue it as coin at £3:17:10½ an ounce. On so large a sum, that meant a loss of between two and a half and three per cent. on the coinage. So even though the bank paid no seignorage, and even though the government properly bore the cost of the coinage, this government generosity did not relieve the bank of all expense.

Because of the same kind of excess, the Scotch banks were all forced to keep agents permanently stationed in London to collect money for them, at a cost that was rarely below one and a half or two per cent. The money was sent up by waggon and insured by the carriers at a further charge of three quarters per cent., or fifteen shillings on every hundred pounds. The agents could not always refill their employers' tills as fast as they were drained. When that happened, the banks fell back on drawing bills of exchange on their London correspondents for whatever sum they needed. Later, when those correspondents drew on them in return for the same sum plus interest and commission, some of the banks were in such distress from their own excessive circulation that the only way they could meet the demand was by drawing a second set of bills, either on the same correspondents or on others in London. In this way the same sum, or rather bills for the same sum, sometimes travelled the round trip two or three times over, with the debtor bank paying interest and commission on the whole accumulated total each time. Even Scotch banks that were never notorious for recklessness were sometimes driven to this ruinous device.

When the Bank of England or the Scotch banks paid out gold coin in exchange for the share of their paper that exceeded what the country's circulation could use, that gold was itself surplus to the circulation. Some of it was shipped abroad as coin, some was melted down and shipped abroad as bullion, and some was melted down and sold back to the Bank of England at the high price of four pounds an ounce. Only the newest, heaviest, and best pieces were carefully picked out of the whole stock and either sent abroad or melted down. At home, so long as they kept the form of coin, these heavy pieces were worth no more than the light ones; but they were worth more abroad, or once melted into bullion at home. So despite all its annual coining, the Bank of England found to its astonishment that there was the same shortage of coin every year as there had been the year before, and that, despite the large quantity of good new coin it issued each year, the overall state of the coinage grew steadily worse rather than better. Every year it had to coin nearly the same amount of gold as the year before, and because the price of gold bullion kept rising as the coin was continually worn and clipped, the cost of this enormous annual coinage rose higher every year. Note too that, by keeping its own tills supplied with coin, the Bank of England is indirectly obliged to supply the whole kingdom, since coin flows out from those tills into the country in countless ways. So whatever coin was needed to sustain this excessive circulation of Scotch and English paper, and whatever gaps that excessive circulation tore in the kingdom's stock of necessary coin, the Bank of England had to make good. The Scotch banks, of course, all paid dearly for their own imprudence and carelessness; but the Bank of England paid dearly not only for its own imprudence but for the far greater imprudence of nearly every Scotch bank.
The original cause of this excessive circulation of paper money was the over-trading of a few bold speculators in both parts of the united kingdom.

What a bank can properly lend a merchant, or an undertaker of any kind, is not the whole capital he trades with, nor even any large part of it. It is only the portion he would otherwise have to keep idle and in ready money to meet occasional demands. So long as the paper money the bank advances never exceeds that amount, it can never exceed the value of the gold and silver that would necessarily circulate in the country if there were no paper money at all; it can never exceed what the country's circulation can easily absorb and put to use.

When a bank discounts a real bill of exchange for a merchant, one drawn by a real creditor on a real debtor, and actually paid by that debtor as soon as it falls due, the bank is only advancing part of the value the merchant would otherwise have to keep idle and in ready money for occasional demands. When the bill is paid at maturity, it restores to the bank the value it advanced, together with the interest. As long as a bank deals only with such customers, its tills are like a pond: a stream runs out of it continually, but another stream runs in just as continually, fully matching the outflow, so that without any further effort the pond stays always full, or very nearly so. Such a bank needs to spend little or nothing to keep its tills replenished.

Even without over-trading, a merchant may often need ready money when he has no bills to discount. Suppose that, on top of discounting his bills, a bank also advances him sums on such occasions through a cash account, and accepts repayment piecemeal as money comes in from the occasional sale of his goods, on the easy terms the banking companies of Scotland offer. Then he no longer needs to keep any part of his stock idle and in ready money for occasional demands. When such demands actually arise, he can meet them from his cash account. In dealing with such a customer, however, the bank must watch closely whether, over some short stretch of time, say four, five, six, or eight months, the repayments it normally receives from him fully match the advances it normally makes to him. If, over such short periods, the repayments from a given customer usually equal the advances, the bank can safely keep dealing with him. The stream running out of its tills in his case may be very large, but the stream running in must be at least as large, so that without further trouble the tills are likely to stay always full, or very nearly so, and almost never require any extraordinary outlay to refill them. If, on the other hand, the repayments from some other customer regularly fall far short of the advances made to him, the bank cannot safely keep dealing with him, at least not on these terms. In his case the outflow from the tills is necessarily much larger than the inflow, so that unless they are refilled by some great and continual effort and expense, the tills must soon run dry altogether.

Accordingly, the banking companies of Scotland were for a long time very careful to require frequent and regular repayments from all their customers, and refused to deal with anyone, however large his fortune or credit, who did not make what they called frequent and regular operations with them. Besides almost entirely saving the extraordinary cost of refilling their tills, this care gave them two other very substantial advantages.

First, it let them form a reasonable judgment about whether their debtors were thriving or declining, without having to look for any evidence beyond their own books, since people generally repay either regularly or irregularly according to whether their affairs are thriving or failing. A private man who lends his money to perhaps six or a dozen debtors can, himself or through his agents, watch and inquire constantly and carefully into the conduct and situation of each of them. But a banking company lending to perhaps five hundred different people, with its attention constantly taken up by quite other matters, can have no reliable information about the conduct and circumstances of most of its debtors beyond what its own books supply. In requiring frequent and regular repayments from all their customers, the banking companies of Scotland probably had this advantage in mind.

Second, this care protected them from the danger of issuing more paper money than the country's circulation could easily absorb and use. When they saw that, over moderate stretches of time, a particular customer's repayments usually equalled the advances they had made to him, they could be sure that the paper they had advanced to him had at no point exceeded the gold and silver he would otherwise have had to keep on hand for occasional demands, and that the paper they had circulated through him had therefore never exceeded the gold and silver that would have circulated in the country had there been no paper money at all. The frequency, regularity, and size of his repayments proved well enough that their advances had at no time exceeded that part of his capital which he would otherwise have had to keep idle and in ready money for occasional demands, that is, the part he keeps free in order to keep the rest of his capital constantly at work. It is only this part of his capital that, over moderate periods, keeps coming back to a trader in the shape of money, whether paper or coin, and keeps going out again in the same shape. If the bank's advances had regularly exceeded this part of his capital, his ordinary repayments could not, over moderate periods, have matched the ordinary advances. The stream that ran into the bank's tills through his dealings could not have equalled the stream that ran out through those same dealings. Once the bank's paper advances exceeded the gold and silver he would otherwise have had to keep for occasional demands, they might soon come to exceed the whole quantity of gold and silver that (assuming the same volume of commerce) would have circulated in the country with no paper money, and so exceed what the country's circulation could easily absorb and use; and the excess paper would immediately return to the bank to be exchanged for gold and silver. This second advantage, though just as real as the first, was perhaps not so well understood by all the different banking companies in Scotland.

Once the discounting of bills and the use of cash accounts together free a country's creditworthy traders from any need to keep part of their stock idle and in ready money for occasional demands, they can reasonably expect no further help from banks and bankers, who, having gone that far, cannot go any further without endangering their own interest and safety. A bank cannot, consistently with its own interest, advance a trader the whole, or even the greater part, of the circulating capital he trades with. That capital does keep returning to him as money and going out again in the same shape, but the full inflow of returns lags too far behind the full outflow of payments, so his repayments could not match his advances within the moderate periods a bank needs. Still less could a bank afford to advance any large part of his fixed capital: the capital an ironmaster, say, sinks into building his forge and smelting-houses, workshops, and warehouses, and the cottages of his workmen; the capital a mine owner sinks into digging shafts, erecting pumping engines, and laying roads and waggon-ways; the capital a man improving land sinks into clearing, draining, fencing, manuring, and ploughing waste and uncultivated fields, and into building farmhouses with their necessary stables, granaries, and the rest. The returns on fixed capital are in almost every case much slower than those on circulating capital, and such outlays, even when made with the greatest prudence and judgment, very seldom come back to the undertaker until after many years, a span far too long to suit a bank. Traders and other undertakers may, quite properly, carry on a large part of their projects with borrowed money. But in fairness to their creditors, their own capital should be enough to secure, so to speak, the creditors' capital, or to make it extremely unlikely that those creditors would lose anything even if the project fell far short of expectations. And even with that precaution, money that is borrowed and meant to stay unrepaid for several years should not be borrowed from a bank. It should be borrowed on bond or mortgage from private people who mean to live on the interest of their money, without troubling to employ the capital themselves, and who are therefore willing to lend it to people of good credit likely to hold it for several years. A bank that lends without the cost of stamped paper or of attorneys' fees for drawing up bonds and mortgages, and that accepts repayment on the easy terms of the Scotch banking companies, would no doubt be a very convenient creditor for such traders and undertakers. But such traders and undertakers would certainly be most inconvenient debtors for such a bank.

It is now more than twenty-five years since the paper money issued by the various banking companies of Scotland was fully equal to, or rather somewhat more than equal to, what the country's circulation could easily absorb and use. So those companies had long since given the traders and other undertakers of Scotland all the help that banks and bankers can give consistently with their own interest. They had even gone a little further. They had over-traded slightly, and had brought on themselves the loss, or at least the reduced profit, that in this business always attends even the smallest degree of over-trading. The traders and undertakers, having got so much help from banks and bankers, wanted still more. They seem to have thought that the banks could extend credit to whatever sum was wanted at no further cost than a few reams of paper. They complained of the narrow views and timid spirit of the bank directors, who, they said, did not extend credit in proportion to the growth of the country's trade, by which they really meant the growth of their own projects beyond what they could carry on with their own capital or with what they could borrow from private people in the usual way of bond or mortgage. The banks, they seemed to think, were in honour bound to make up the shortfall and supply them with all the capital they wanted to trade with. The banks took a different view, however, and when they refused to extend credit, some of these traders resorted to a device that served their purpose for a while, at much greater expense but just as effectively as the fullest extension of bank credit could have done. This device was nothing but the well-known shift of drawing and redrawing, the trick that failing traders sometimes resort to when they are on the brink of bankruptcy. Raising money this way had long been known in England, and during the late war, when high trading profits offered a great temptation to over-trade, it is said to have been practised on a very large scale. From England it was brought to Scotland, where, in proportion to the country's very limited commerce and very modest capital, it was soon carried much further than it ever had been in England.

The practice of drawing and redrawing is so familiar to every man of business that it may seem pointless to explain it. But since this book may reach many readers who are not in business, and since the effect of the practice on the banking trade is perhaps not generally understood even by businessmen themselves, I will try to explain it as plainly as I can.

The customs of merchants were established when Europe's crude laws did not enforce contracts, and over the last two centuries they have been written into the laws of every European nation. They give bills of exchange such extraordinary privileges that money is advanced on them more readily than on any other kind of obligation, especially when they are made payable within so short a period as two or three months after their date. If, when the bill falls due, the acceptor does not pay it the moment it is presented, he is from that moment a bankrupt. The bill is protested and goes back to the drawer, who likewise becomes a bankrupt if he does not pay it at once. If, before reaching the person who finally presents it to the acceptor for payment, the bill had passed through the hands of several other people, who had successively advanced its value to one another in money or goods, and who, to show that each had in turn received that value, had each in order endorsed it, that is, written his name on the back, then each endorser becomes in his turn liable to the holder for the value, and if he fails to pay he too becomes a bankrupt from that moment. Even if the drawer, acceptor, and endorsers are all people of doubtful credit, the shortness of the term still gives the holder some security. They may all be very likely to go bankrupt, but the odds are against all of them doing so within so short a time. The house is shaky, a tired traveller says to himself, and will not stand much longer; but the odds are against its falling tonight, so I'll risk sleeping in it tonight.

Suppose trader A in Edinburgh draws a bill on B in London, payable two months after date. In fact B in London owes A nothing, but B agrees to accept A's bill on condition that, before it falls due, B may redraw on A in Edinburgh for the same sum plus interest and a commission, in another bill likewise payable two months after date. So before the first two months are up, B redraws this bill on A in Edinburgh; then, before the second two months are up, A draws another bill on B in London, again payable two months after date; and before the third two months are up, B redraws on A another bill, also payable two months after date. This could go on not only for months but for years at a stretch, the bill always coming back to A in Edinburgh with the accumulated interest and commission of all the earlier bills piled on. The interest was five per cent. a year, and the commission was never less than one half per cent. on each draught. Since the commission was charged more than six times a year, whatever money A raised this way must have cost him something over eight per cent. a year, and sometimes a great deal more, when either the commission rate rose or he had to pay compound interest on the interest and commission of earlier bills. This practice was called raising money by circulation.

In a country where the ordinary profits on most mercantile projects are reckoned to run between six and ten per cent., it must have been a very lucky venture indeed whose returns could not only repay the enormous cost at which the money was borrowed to carry it on, but leave a good surplus profit for the projector besides. Yet many vast and ambitious projects were launched and kept going for years with no other backing than money raised at this enormous expense. In their golden dreams the projectors no doubt saw this great profit vividly. But when they woke, either at the end of their projects or when they could no longer keep them going, they very seldom, I believe, had the luck to find it.

{The method described in the text was by no means the most common or the most expensive way these adventurers sometimes raised money by circulation. It often happened that A in Edinburgh would enable B in London to pay the first bill of exchange by drawing, a few days before it fell due, a second bill at three months' date on the same B in London. Made payable to his own order, A sold this bill in Edinburgh at par, and used the proceeds to buy bills on London payable at sight to the order of B, which he sent to B by post. Towards the end of the late war the exchange between Edinburgh and London was often three per cent. against Edinburgh, so these sight bills must often have cost A that premium. Repeated at least four times a year, and burdened each time with a commission of at least one half per cent., this transaction must at that period have cost A at least fourteen per cent. a year. At other times A would clear the first bill by drawing, a few days before it fell due, a second bill at two months' date, not on B but on some third person, C, say, in London. This bill was made payable to the order of B, who, once C had accepted it, discounted it with some banker in London; and A enabled C to clear it by drawing, a few days before it fell due, a third bill, likewise at two months' date, sometimes on his first correspondent B and sometimes on some fourth or fifth person, D or E, say. Repeated at least six times a year, and burdened each time with a commission of at least one half per cent. on top of the legal interest of five per cent., this method of raising money, like the one described in the text, must have cost A something over eight per cent.
